Détente was its negotiated re-entry into the community of nations, and since then, the reforms undertaken within China propelled it to becoming a global power. Iran’s story differs from this in the sense that it is not going to be a global power. However, it is certainly going to emerge as a regional power in a very important region of the world. Second, Iran’s re-entry into the world community is going to be far more disorderly than that of China, mainly because it has had to fight its way out of the oblivion into which it was banished since the revolution of 1979. Short of an attempt to destroy its infrastructure, Iran’s emergence as a big power in the region is unstoppable. But emergence is now underway. It will be a very disorderly, and possibly violent, affair. A lot depends on which faction within Iran manages to rise to the top and take over decision-making. In China, an internal reckoning took place within the Communist Party first, before the reform-minded elements around Deng Xiaoping could rise to the top and take control of the post-opening up trajectory. That is a fraught history, from the Cultural Revolution and the purge of Deng in 1966, to the attempted coup by Lin Biao and his death in a plane crash in Mongolia in 1971, to the rise of Zhou Enlai and the so-called Gang of Four that was ranged against him and the eventual emergence of Deng as the successor, his second purge after Zhou Enlai’s death, and eventual restoration following Mao’s death in 1976. That is when China firmly embarked on its reformist course and broke its moorings to Mao’s thought. What followed was a carefully calibrated set of measures designed to open the Chinese economy up to the outside world — slowly and experimentally. That trajectory eventually propelled China towards becoming a global power, even if the process took many decades to complete. Iran is now at a similar point in its trajectory. Following the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and its victory in the war against the Zionist alliance of America and Israel, it now has to go through the internal process of wrangling between rival factions, who must decide whether to remain wedded to the past or break out into a new future. This process will take years to unfold; what makes the Iranian trajectory different from the Chinese one is that in Iran the process will unfold in the context of a war. It is evident that within Iran there is a pragmatic faction that wants to see the war come to a close and the task of rebuilding the country to begin. But equally important, there is a faction that wants to press ahead with the fighting to deliver a humiliating defeat to the aggressors. This faction wants to do to the Americans in the Middle East what the Taliban, too, did to them in Afghanistan: force a hurried and disorderly flight from the region. The real game begins after that. Once the Americans leave the region, the Iranian military machine will turn its attention towards the Gulf monarchs. There will be reparations to pay. The bill for the war has already been served. In July 2025, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Financial Times that there could be no return to nuclear talks until Iran had been compensated for the damage caused by the June war. America scoffed at the demand. In March 2026, the demand was made again in the counter-offer that Iran made to the American proposal for talks. In April, they added an amount — $270 billion — while another figure of $300bn was written into the US-Iran MOU in June 2026. Nobody should be scoffing at the demand now. In addition to retaining control of Hormuz, Iran will press this demand in the days to come and it is the Gulf monarchs who will be left to pay the bill once the US decides the conflict no longer serves any of its interests. And once the Gulf monarchs settle this amount, another will surface. And then another. Iran’s emergence as a big power in the region is now unstoppable, short of an attempted catastrophic destruction of the entire country’s infrastructure by the Zionist alliance. This may be an unlikely outcome at this point in time, but it cannot be ruled out. The emergence as a big power is already underway. After consolidating their control on Hormuz, they will next turn their gaze to the riches of the Gulf monarchs. Those riches are now imperilled. China’s story is instructive here because it tells us that a post-revolutionary polity can manage its affairs to secure its re-entry into the global system of trade, finance and diplomacy to procure maximum benefits for itself. Whether Iran manages this moment similarly, or whether they decide to press their military advantage to the hilt and use their newfound centrality to avenge the past rather than build a future, is the big question hanging over all of us today. The writer is a business and economy journalist. khurram.husain@gmail.com X: @khurramhusain Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no.headline: DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no regional aspirations', intended for collective deterrence
DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no.summary: Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that the Makkah Defence Alliance — a tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye — has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence. The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson. During the show, aired during the early hours of Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked about Pakistan’s commitments under the agreement. “It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said. Watson then asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”. Elaborating further, he said the countries part of the alliance had independent relationships with other nations, blocs and alliances. “So this mutual defence agreement is complementary in nature. It is not competing with any other relationship of these countries,” he added. At that, Watson asked, “But does it contain any mutual defence obligation?” In his short reply to the question, Lt Gen Chaudhry remarked, “The text that has been made public by the leadership of the three countries enunciates that very clearly and it’s interpretation is quite clear.” Asked how Pakistan would respond if one of the countries in the alliance came under attack, he said that the operationalisation of defensive commitments was never made public in any discourse. “You see, you have multiple other agreements which are defensive in nature, which are committal in nature. But no country comes out and starts sharing its operational details […] What you’re asking is the how part — that how we are going to defend Pakistan against any aggression. “That is always part of the operational classification and security […] What you’re asking is that how it will be done. It is for the three countries to decide, and it is for them to know and for them to actualise it,” he said. Specifically asked whether the military spokesperson saw the alliance “complementing or competing” with Pakistan’s relationship with China, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that it complemented Islamabad-Beijing ties. “We need to understand that the Pak-Saudi and the Pak-Turkiye relationship has not come out of the blue. The Chinese understand it. The world at large understands it. That’s how historic these relationships are. We have formalised that. “Nobody has any problem with that. Everyone understands that this is defensive. Everyone understands it is for maintaining stability and peace in the region. And all the three countries that are part of it, they have a wonderful relationship with China,” he said. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture. He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability. “It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. “This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence. “But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated. The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo. From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point. The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained. US-Iran mediation and Pakistan’s ‘unique position’ During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked about Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between the United States and Iran and whether the Makkah Defence Alliance complicated Islamabad’s position towards Tehran. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied such was not the case, adding that the alliance was based on decades-old strategic ties. “This alliance is a formalisation of that strategic relationship in a peculiar environment,” he said, reiterating that the pact was based on collective deterrence. The defence pact, he said, had no offensive or aggressive element and was purely defensive in nature. Asked why Pakistan had opted to play the role of a mediator in the ongoing Middle East conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, he succinctly stated, “For regional peace.” Lt Gen Chaudhry then added that stability stemmed from peace and Pakistan was a proponent of peace in the region. Moreover, he continued, Pakistan had a “unique position” in this case because of its policy of alignment and engagement with countries across the world. Hence, it could play the role of an “objective arbiter of peace and an honest broker of peace”. To a question about progress on the mediation front and towards a settlement, Lt Gen Chaudhry explained that one of the prerequisites of good mediation was remaining objective and neutral. “So it’s not for us as a mediator to start commenting on things that are happening or that are bound to happen,” he said, adding that Pakistan’s political and military leadership had been reaching out to all the parties so that “better sense prevails and, instead of a military solution, we come to a negotiated outcome of this very complex situation”. Watson then pointed to the possibility of the US and Iran rejecting Pakistan’s proposal and asked whether Islamabad was prepared to continue its mediation in that case. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied, “Is there any other way of resolving this conflict other than [through] mediation? Is there any other desirable way of doing that?” He stressed the need for a “negotiated, peaceful outcome”, adding that those who could mediate objectively and sincerely between the two sides must continue their efforts. Asked whether Pakistan was concerned about the conflict spilling over towards its western frontiers, Lt Gen Chaudhry answered that as far as Pakistan’s borders, territorial integrity and sovereignty were concerned, “we are very confident and very self-reliant on our security”. There were always concerns of any conflict spiralling horizontally or vertically, he said, adding that not just Pakistan, but the entire world at large was feeling the impact of the conflict. “So, there are [always] concerns in multiple domains”, but Pakistan was “fully confident of taking care of whatever nefarious designs come out of that towards” it, he said. Asked whether Pakistan aimed to become a regional mediator or was simply trying to prevent a regional war from reaching its own doorstep, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Pakistan is interested in regional peace and stability, because peace and stability are essential for development, for human development, for prosperity and for the citizens of Pakistan and the region.” And if the “mediation is for peace, […] and we’ll always be there”. Prospects of dialogue with India Watson then came to the brief military conflict between Pakistan and India in May last year, and asked what lessons Pakistan’s military had learned from the episode. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied that what was more important were the lessons Pakistan and its military taught during that conflict. He said that a military conflict between two nuclear countries, especially neighbours, was “out of question”. “It’s a sheer, I would say, a sort of mad idea,” he said, adding that Pakistan also showed that India made a “strategic folly” in May last year. Asked whether he believed India had learned that lesson, Lt Gen Chaudhry replied it was for the Indian side to answer. “Our job in Pakistan is to keep on reminding them of that lesson,” he said, adding that the other side had a “hubristic mindset” and the Indian military was “deeply politicised”. In India, he continued, there was a propensity of externalising their internal problems, giving the example of minorities facing oppression. On the other hand, he said, there was the Kashmir issue, which was an “external problem” that New Delhi wanted to “internalise through repression”. The military’s spokesperson added that Pakistan continued to give out the message to India that it believed in “peace on equal terms” and that it was a rational and objective player. Pakistan believes in regional peace, but if India has any “misconceptions about [imposing] regional hegemony through military aggression, results of that would be beyond their imagination”, he warned. Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan had showed India and the world in May last year that it had the capability and resolve to dominate and control an escalation. “And we’ll do it again,” he added. Asked whether there were any realistic prospects of restoring sustained military-to-military communication with India, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Yes, of course.” He added that communication between the directors general of military operations had remained effective during the May conflict and beyond. “Communication is always good. We must communicate, we must engage, but that engagement has to be done on equal terms while respecting each other’s integrity and sovereignty,” he said. To a question about resuming dialogue with India, he said it was for the political leadership to decide. But dialogue, he said, had to be on equal terms. “Dialogue cannot be, or engagement cannot be to provide a cover for the ongoing state-sponsored Indian terrorism in Pakistan, for the ongoing aggression,” he emphasised. ‘Only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world’ Coming to Afghanistan, Watson asked about the Pakistani military’s preferred end state with the Afghan Taliban. “I think the military’s end state is actually part of Pakistan’s end state that the political leadership sets. So, there is no separate military end state. “So, there are Pakistan’s objectives and desire, which are primarily the domain of the Pakistan’s political leadership and an expression of the will of the people of Pakistan. And what that is that we want — no interference, no terrorism from Afghanistan in Pakistan. So that’s the foundation,” he said. Asked what options Pakistan considered legitimate for preventing cross-border attacks in case of the failure of diplomacy, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Right of self-defence is enshrined in the Article 51 of the United Nations; right of self-defence is given to each nation state of the world.” He added that the Pakistani state had an obligation to defend the lives, honour and property of its citizens. To that end, “all that is necessary will be done and is being done”. In this connection, he detailed Pakistan’s counter-terrorism measures and said the country’s counter-terrorism campaign was the “only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world”. “Because we are the bulwark state against” terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, he said. Lt Gen Chaudhry also mentioned that in the current year, 42,000 intelligence-based operations (IBOs) had been carried out and 2,100 terrorists had been killed. Towards the programme’s end, Watson steered the discussion towards Balochistan, on which Lt Gen Chaudhry said there was no insurgency in the province. “There’s just terrorism,” he said, adding that the military had clarity on that, tactically and strategically. He said of the 42,000 IBOs, over 32,000 were conducted in Balochistan and security forces remained engaged in “taking out the so-called proxies who associate themselves with Balochistan and have got nothing to do with it”. Regarding strategic clarity, he said the government, people of Balochistan and the military understood that the way to deal with terrorism was to kill terrorists and “embrace the people of Balochistan”.

JI chief warns talks with govt may end a.headline: JI chief warns talks with govt may end after 4th round if decision on abolishing petroleum levy delayed
JI chief warns talks with govt may end a.summary: KARACHI: Jamaat-i-Islami Pakistan (JI) Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Wednesday warned that ongoing talks with the government over the petroleum levy may end if the levy is not withdrawn soon. The talks between the government and JI began on September 7 after the two sides agreed to form committees, comprising experts and leaders, to discuss recommendations for reducing the petroleum levy and providing relief to the public. So far, three rounds of talks have been held, with the fourth round scheduled for 6pm today (Wednesday) in Islamabad. According to a statement issued by the party, the JI chief spoke in Karachi earlier in the day, where he rejected the government’s fuel relief scheme and demanded that the levy be abolished, “rather than replaced with temporary relief schemes”. “If the government continues delaying and does not abolish the petroleum levy, today’s talks will be the last round,” Rehman was quoted as saying, reiterating that the party will go ahead with its march to Islamabad on Sept 20. As per the statement, Rehman said the government collected Rs1,567 billion through the petroleum levy annually but announced only Rs25bn in relief for the public. He described the package as inadequate and questioned its proposed implementation through weekly fuel distribution, the statement added. Rehman slammed “lockdown measures”. He added that the traders were “being pressured in the name of maintaining the system”. As per the statement, Rehman “called for an end to the practice of revising petroleum prices daily”. He voiced concern at the “frequent revisions”, which he said created difficulties for consumers and businesses. Speaking to the media, Rehman also outlined plans to hold “public meetings”, adding that a “large gathering” would be held in Karachi on Wednesday night, followed by rallies in Lahore on Thursday, and in Mardan and Peshawar on Friday. “The Islamabad march will not stop,” he was quoted as saying. Rehman urged the government not to disrupt peaceful and democratic struggle, according to the statement. Meanwhile, in a post on X, the party said that Wednesday’s round will be held in the Federal Secretariat at 6pm, with the JI delegation led by Liaquat Baloch and the government by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal. The government’s team will also include Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani. JI has been staging regular sit-ins in Lahore, Peshawar, Karachi and dozens of other locations across the country since August 16 to protest the levy and IPP agreements. The government levies Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Last week, the JI chief had warned the government that the ongoing protest would march towards Islamabad on September 20 if the levy was not withdrawn.

OpenAI's rogue agents probed Hugging Fac.headline: OpenAI's rogue agents probed Hugging Face for weaknesses 2 months before major hack
OpenAI's rogue agents probed Hugging Fac.summary: Rogue AI agents from OpenAI hijacked Hugging Face user accounts and probed the site itself for vulnerabilities as early as May, nearly two months before the July breach of the open-source repository drew global attention, according to researchers who reviewed the activity. The newly uncovered malicious activity showed that the rogue agents’ efforts to find a way into Hugging Face began earlier than publicly known. OpenAI had previously disclosed one aspect of the malicious activity — the theft of a Hugging Face user’s digital credential to access a biology-related file — in its public incident report last month, but researchers told Reuters the probing activity against Hugging Face appeared to go beyond what was described in the report. The activity was discovered by independent researcher Jonas Wiedermann-Moeller last week, he told Reuters. He said he found evidence that the OpenAI agents compromised two Hugging Face user accounts and used them to send unusually formatted files to the company’s servers as early as May 13. He and other researchers who reviewed the evidence said the behaviour resembled an attempt to map or test parts of Hugging Face’s network for ways to infiltrate, although they stressed there was no evidence the effort resulted in an actual breach. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had disclosed the May 13 event, privately notified Hugging Face about the activity flagged by Wiedermann-Moeller and was “committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as our review continues.” Hugging Face, recently acquired by chipmaker Nvidia, did not respond to requests for comment. Wiedermann-Moeller, a 27-year-old who lives in Bielefeld, Germany, said OpenAI’s failure to detect the May 13 probing at the time was a missed opportunity to prevent the subsequent hacking campaign, which has triggered a global reckoning over the power of artificial intelligence. “Imagine if they caught this behaviour in May,” he said in an interview. “It could’ve prevented the later incident, which was way bigger.” OpenAI has previously said that, with the benefit of hindsight, “some early signals” from its AI agents should have triggered an earlier response. ‘Clear warning sign’ Two outside experts who reviewed Wiedermann-Moeller’s findings said they were consistent with activity previously linked to OpenAI’s agents. SentinelOne senior threat researcher Tom Hegel said the account hijacking and subsequent probing matched known behaviour by the agents “to a tee.” Sydney Von Arx of the Nightingale Collective, an AI safety group, agreed with the attribution. Von Arx said the hacking amounted to a “clear warning sign” that could have helped prevent the breach in July. OpenAI has faced increasing scrutiny since the company disclosed on July 21 that rogue AI agents bypassed internal controls, reached the open internet and coordinated actions that OpenAI described as “an unprecedented cyber incident.” Since then, outside researchers have identified additional incidents alleged to involve OpenAI-linked agents, including activity affecting a dormant German wiki site and the RubyGems software package repository. OpenAI has acknowledged some of those incidents only after they were publicly reported by third parties. Two people familiar with the matter said that, in the case of RubyGems, OpenAI employees only realised its AI was responsible for the malicious activity after the Nightingale Collective found it. The additional discoveries have fueled questions among lawmakers and AI safety advocates about whether the full scope of the incidents has been identified. Some of America’s top AI executives have since called for a slowdown of AI development, citing, among other things, the threat of devastating cyberattacks by out-of-control agents. Wiedermann-Moeller said the latest findings reinforced calls for a temporary slowdown in the development of advanced AI systems. “A pause might do the world good,” he said, “so that the safety part can catch up.”

story_clusters.representative_headline: Petroleum dealers demand govt devise mechanism for fuel subsidy reimbursement

articles.headline: Petroleum dealers demand govt devise mechanism for fuel subsidy reimbursement
articles.summary: KARACHI: Petroleum dealers have called on the government to devise a mechanism for reimbursing the fuel subsidy, which is set to take effect across the country from midnight on Wednesday. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Under the scheme, a relief of Rs100 per litre on a monthly quota of 20 litres will be provided to bike and auto owners, while those owning small vehicles of up to 800cc will get a relief of Rs100 per litre for a monthly quota of 30 litres. “We welcome the government’s move for the benefit of the public, but our businesses should not suffer,” Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) Chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh said. He was addressing an emergency press conference on Wednesday along with other office-bearers of the association. “The fuel subsidy scheme started in Islamabad at midnight on Tuesday and will be launched across the country from tonight,” Malik said. He added: “But our issue is that petroleum dealers are asking us: who will pay the subsidy amount and when?” He explained that no fuel station could afford to bear a loss of Rs100 per litre or wait for delayed payments for a long period. “We have approached the Petroleum Division, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) and even the Finance Ministry to get an answer to one simple question,” Khuda Bakhsh said. He added that the confusion was compounded by the fact that it appeared none of the authorities themselves were aware of the issue. “The officials of Ogra and oil marketing companies say that the Petroleum Division will possibly pay the subsidy amount, whereas Petroleum Division officials maintain that the payments will be made by the Finance Ministry. A Finance Ministry official has assured us that the State Bank will release the funds within a day or two,” he added. He also maintained that the federal government had assured the dealers that they would be taken into confidence before the launch of the fuel relief package. “The government has to understand that if payments are not reimbursed on time, many dealers will stop participating in the scheme, as many previous promises made by the government were not fulfilled,” he added. PPDA Vice Chairman Tariq Hassan said that around 14,000 dealers across the country had been trying to contact the government for the past three days, but whenever the government wanted to enforce something, it stopped communication. Another vice chairman, Anwar Kamal, said that if the scheme was to be successful, the government must negotiate with dealers. He also rejected the government’s proposed “smart lockdown”. He added that billions of rupees belonging to dealers should not remain tied up for a long period under the scheme. Meanwhile, Minister Shaza Fatima announced on Wednesday night that the issue related to the forwarding of SMS messages from preloaded packages and low balances had been resolved. “The prime minister has made the SMS for the fuel subsidy available free of charge, and Jazz has completed the system shift. Other telecom companies will also do so by Thursday,” she added.

articles.headline: Dealers await answers as fuel subsidy rollout begins
articles.summary: • Petroleum dealers lament lack of clarity on payment mechanism, timeline• PM wants facilitation desks to help people trying to buy subsidised fuel• Ogra attributes hike to elevated crude prices despite decline in int’l rates ISLAMABAD: Even as members of the public who have signed up for the PM’s Fuel Relief Scheme queued up at fuel pumps late on Wednesday night, petroleum dealers were still not clear about the mechanism whereby they would be compensated. The concern was voiced by the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) during a presser in Karachi, where its chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh said that no fuel pump could afford to bear a loss of Rs100 per litre without clarity on how they will be compensated. He claimed that between the petroleum ministry, Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) and even the finance ministry, no one had been able to answer their questions. “Officials from Ogra and oil marketing companies say that the petroleum ministry will possibly pay the subsidy amount, whereas ministry officials maintain that payments will be made by the finance ministry, while finance ministry officials assure us that the State Bank will release the funds in a day or two,“ Mr Bakhsh added. A day earlier, the National Steering Com­mittee on Fuel Subsidy — chaired by Deputy PM Ishaq Dar — had ordered that payments to fuel stations under the PM’s scheme be processed within 24 hours through the State Bank of Pakistan. However, Mr Bakhsh said the federal government had assured dealers that they would be taken into confidence before the launch of the fuel relief package, but lamented that no such consultation took place. ”The government has to understand that if payments are not reimbursed in time, many dealers will stop participating in [the scheme], as many previous promises were also not fulfilled by the government,” he added. PPDA Vice Chairman Tariq Hassan said that around 14,000 dealers across the country have been trying desperately to contact the government over the past three days, adding that whenever Islamabad wants to enforce something, it stops communication. Another vice chairman, Anwar Kamal, said that if the scheme was to be successful, the government must negotiate with dealers, adding that dealers could not afford to have billions tied up for a long period under this scheme. Mr Bakhsh later told Dawn they had been invited to a virtual meeting with the relevant federal secretary on Thursday morning. He added that Ogra officials had also reached out to brief him, but he had asked for that information in writing, so he could relay that to the members of his association. Facilitation desks Earlier, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered authorities to set up facilitation desks comprising administration officials, volunteers and petrol pump staff to assist citizens in easily obtaining fuel subsidy under the special relief scheme, which was rolled out across the country at Wednesday midnight, following the launch of the pilot phase in Islamabad. Presiding over a meeting to review progress on the scheme, PM Shehbaz directed that personnel deployed at the facilitation desks should guide eligible citizens and provide them with all possible assistance in registration and other necessary procedures. The prime minister also asked the relevant authorities to remain proactive in creating public awareness about the scheme, which will benefit people from all four provinces, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. The meeting was informed that the scheme had been designed in a simple and easy-to-understand manner for the public. Only four pieces of information were required for registration: the applicant’s CNIC number, vehicle number plate, province of registration and vehicle registration date. Complete details of the fuel subsidy scheme are available in Urdu on www.pmfuelrelief.pk. According to an official, the number of successful registrations was gradually rising, while provincial governments were extending “full cooperation” for nationwide implementation of the scheme. Oil prices Meanwhile, notifying fresh POL rates on Wednesday night, Ogra attributed the steep hikes to elevated international crude oil and petroleum product prices. The price of high-speed diesel was increased by Rs5.62 per litre to Rs421.45, while petrol became costlier by Rs6.88 per litre, taking its new price to Rs391.22 per litre. However, Reuters reported on Wednesday night that oil prices fell in the open market on reports that Saudi Arabia was offering additional crude cargoes through Oman eased some concerns about Middle East supply disruptions. Brent crude futures fell $2.92, or 2.7 per cent, to settle at $105.83 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate futures fell $3.40, or 3.2pc, to close at $102.43, Reuters reported. Saudi Arabia is offering more loadings of crude oil to Asian refiners via ship-to-ship transfers off Oman’s Sohar port, people familiar with the matter said, blunting some of the hit to global supply from attacks on the country’s East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. Oil prices had gained more than $3 in the previous session after shipping industry sources said crude loadings at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea export hub of Yanbu had been suspended and Riyadh had cancelled some cargo deliveries to European customers. The suspension followed strikes on the East-West pipeline, which feeds the Saudi port of Yanbu. It became the main Saudi outlet for oil exports after Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz after US and Israeli attacks on the country. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

articles.headline: Petroleum dealers demand govt devise mechanism for fuel subsidy reimbursement
articles.summary: KARACHI: Petroleum dealers have called on the government to devise a mechanism for reimbursing the fuel subsidy, which is set to take effect across the country from midnight on Wednesday. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Under the scheme, a relief of Rs100 per litre on a monthly quota of 20 litres will be provided to bike and auto owners, while those owning small vehicles of up to 800cc will get a relief of Rs100 per litre for a monthly quota of 30 litres. “We welcome the government’s move for the benefit of the public, but our businesses should not suffer,” Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) Chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh said. He was addressing an emergency press conference on Wednesday along with other office-bearers of the association. “The fuel subsidy scheme started in Islamabad at midnight on Tuesday and will be launched across the country from tonight,” Malik said. He added: “But our issue is that petroleum dealers are asking us: who will pay the subsidy amount and when?” He explained that no fuel station could afford to bear a loss of Rs100 per litre or wait for delayed payments for a long period. “We have approached the Petroleum Division, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) and even the Finance Ministry to get an answer to one simple question,” Khuda Bakhsh said. He added that the confusion was compounded by the fact that it appeared none of the authorities themselves were aware of the issue. “The officials of Ogra and oil marketing companies say that the Petroleum Division will possibly pay the subsidy amount, whereas Petroleum Division officials maintain that the payments will be made by the Finance Ministry. A Finance Ministry official has assured us that the State Bank will release the funds within a day or two,” he added. He also maintained that the federal government had assured the dealers that they would be taken into confidence before the launch of the fuel relief package. “The government has to understand that if payments are not reimbursed on time, many dealers will stop participating in the scheme, as many previous promises made by the government were not fulfilled,” he added. PPDA Vice Chairman Tariq Hassan said that around 14,000 dealers across the country had been trying to contact the government for the past three days, but whenever the government wanted to enforce something, it stopped communication. Another vice chairman, Anwar Kamal, said that if the scheme was to be successful, the government must negotiate with dealers. He also rejected the government’s proposed “smart lockdown”. He added that billions of rupees belonging to dealers should not remain tied up for a long period under the scheme. Meanwhile, Minister Shaza Fatima announced on Wednesday night that the issue related to the forwarding of SMS messages from preloaded packages and low balances had been resolved. “The prime minister has made the SMS for the fuel subsidy available free of charge, and Jazz has completed the system shift. Other telecom companies will also do so by Thursday,” she added.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Google-Pakistan deal raises data privacy concerns

articles.headline: Google-Pakistan deal raises data privacy concerns
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD: Media watchdog Freedom Network has penned an open letter to Google and the government, seeking to know what sa­­feguards will ensure that the tech giant’s recent partnership with Pakistan strengthens the country’s digital economy without creating a backdoor for surveillance, censorship or unrestricted access to citizens’ personal information. The Islamabad-based watchdog welcomed the signing of memoranda of understanding and agreements be­­tween Google and the governm­e­­nt after the company opened its of­­fice in Pakistan to advance the country’s digital vision, but expres­sed ap­­prehensions that the tech company and the government had not made details of their agreements public. “A big question is what exactly has been agreed? Will the government or Google publish all MoUs, agreements, contracts or other arra­ngements signed between them? If some provisions must remain confidential, who decided that and under what law?” Freedom Network asked in its alert shared with the media through a press release. The media watchdog asked if there were any undisclosed commitments concerning access to user data, content, metadata or government databases. “Under what circumstances can Pakistani authorities request information about Google users? Will every request require a valid legal process and judicial oversight? Will Google reject requests that are overly broad, vague or inconsistent with fundamental rights?” Media watchdog seeks details of MoUs, agreements Freedom Network was explicit in asking if any protection or unambiguous safeguards against government access to journalists’ Gmail, Google Drive, photos, YouTube accounts, search-related information or other data that could reveal confidential sources were part of the agreements and MoUs. The watchdog asked Google to commit itself to not removing any content merely because a government agency asks, or that requests for blocking or removal shall be assessed under transparent legal standards and users shall receive notice and an opportunity to challenge decisions where legally possible. Freedom Network also worried about where Pakistani citizens’ data would be stored as the country is developing a national data-governance framework that urges data sovereignty, minimum disclosure and citizens’ right to know who has accessed their information. “Will Pakistani users’ data be stored in Pakistan, overseas, or both?” it asked Google. “There should not be informal or undocumented data-sharing arrangements between Google and the Pakistan government.” The press release quoted the media watchdog as asking the tech company: “Who independently will audit Google’s compliance with privacy and human-rights safeguards in Pakistan? The answer should not be simply the government.” Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

story_clusters.representative_headline: CDF Munir, US-based POWERUS discuss defence technology, cooperation

articles.headline: CDF Munir, US-based POWERUS discuss defence technology, cooperation
articles.summary: Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir on Wednesday discussed evolving trends in defence technology and potential areas of cooperation with United States-based defence and critical infrastructure company POWERUS, the military’s media wing said. The meeting focused on opportunities for collaboration in defence procurement, production and capacity building, according to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR). The POWERUS delegation was led by Robert Bret Velicovich. During the meeting, CDF Munir also highlighted the “importance of technological innovation and advanced solutions in strengthening national security and resilience.” The company, according to its website, “builds hardware and unified systems architecture that keep critical assets running in high-consequence environments.” Both sides expressed interest in further developing engagement in areas of mutual interest, added ISPR. In January, US and Pakistan army soldiers completed training at the National Counter-Terrorism Center during Exercise Inspired Gambit, which focused on combined infantry skills and tactics, and counterterrorism operations. In December last year, the US approved the sale of advanced technology and upgrade packages for Pakistan’s F-16 fighter aircraft, a deal valued at approximately $686 million.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Islamabad, Beijing activate joint border commission

articles.headline: Islamabad, Beijing activate joint border commission
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and China on Wednesday operationalised a long pending joint mechanism for managing their common border, with Islamabad des­cribing the move as a significant milestone in bilateral relations and a step toward closer coordination on border management, trade and cross-border connectivity. “The inaugural meeting of the Commission was held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Islamabad,” the Foreign Office said in a statement. The meeting was co-led by Li Ya, deputy director general of the Department of Boundary and Ocean Affairs at China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Bilal Mahmood Chaudhary, director general for China at Pakistan’s Foreign Office. The FO described the ope­r­ationalisation of the Pakis­tan-China Boundary Joint Com­m­ission as a “significant milestone for Pak­istan-China relations”, saying it would set “the stage for enh­anced cooperation in border management, joint border surveys, trade flows and people to people connectivity.” The commission has its origins in the 2013 Agre­ement on the Boundary Mana­gement System signed during the visit of then Chinese Premier Li Keqiang to Islamabad. Article 45 of the agreement provides for establishment of the joint commission to oversee implementation of the border management arrangements. The mechanism would provide an institutional framework for dealing with practical issues along the border, including maintenance and inspection of the boundary, joint surveys, boundary marker issues, management of cross-border facilities and handling of incidents involving the border. Its activation also gives the two countries a mechanism for regular coordination on a border that is important for movement between Pakistan and China, including thr­ough the Khunjerab crossing, and for trade and connectivity linked to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The new commission is distinct from the Joint Boundary Demarcation Commission that was established under the Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement of March 2, 1963. The earlier commission had a specific and essentially one time mandate to conduct surveys, establish boundary markers, prepare detailed maps and set out the alignment of the boundary. Its work ended after the signing of the protocol and maps completing the demarcation process. The 1963 agreement was signed in Beijing by then-Pakistani foreign minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and his Chinese counterpart Chen Yi. It also provided that, following a settlement of the Kashmir dispute between Pakistan and India, the relevant sovereign authority would reopen negotiations with China on the boundary. The 2013 agreement, by contrast, established a continuing system for managing the already demarcated boundary, including provisions for dealing with boundary markers and cross-border infrastructure. The agreement says that if a marker cannot be restored at its original location, the joint commission can determine another suitable location, provided the boundary line itself is not altered. India, which disputes the validity of the 1963 agreement and regards the territory covered by it as part of Occupied Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, rejected the new mechanism. “We have seen reports in this regard. Our position on this matter is clear and consistent. There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis,” Ind­ian Foreign Ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said. For Pakistan and China, however, the commission provides a new institutional arrangement for managing their border relationship and dealing with practical issues that have emerged since the 2013 agreement, while leaving the broader territorial positions of the parties unchanged. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

articles.headline: Govt increases petrol price by Rs6.88 per litre, HSD by Rs5.62 per litre
articles.summary: if (!window._rawHtmlListenerAttached) { window._rawHtmlListenerAttached = true; window.addEventListener('message', function(event) { if (event.data && event.data.type === 'raw-html-resize' && event.data.id) { var iframe = document.getElementById(event.data.id); if (iframe) { var height = Math.min(Math.max(event.data.height, 50), 9200); iframe.style.height = height + 'px'; } } }); } The government on Wednesday increased the price of petrol by Rs6.88 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs5.62 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs391.22 per litre while HSD will cost Rs421.45 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on Sept 17 (Thursday). According to Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA), the increase is primarily linked to higher petrol and diesel prices in the international market. The regulator said the prices were revised based on international market rates, premiums and other relevant factors. The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. A statement from the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said owners of two- and three-wheelers would receive relief of Rs100 per litre on a monthly quota of 20 litres, while owners of vehicles up to 800cc would receive the same relief on a monthly quota of 30 litres. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'practically and diplomatically' if Yemen conflict escalates: Asif

articles.headline: Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'practically and diplomatically' if Yemen conflict escalates: Asif
articles.summary: Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Wednesday said Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated. Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. However, the Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh’s report as a “lie” that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah. “If the situation escalates, we will stand with Saudi Arabia, both practically and diplomatically,” he said while speaking on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shehzaib Khanzada Ke Saath’. Commenting on the Pakistan-Turkiye-Saudi Arabia trilateral agreement — the Makkah Defence Alliance — he affirmed that an agreement was in place. However, he said that even if there had been no such agreement, Pakistan was bound by an “eternal agreement to respond if the holy sites come under attack”. “There are some worldly agreements, too, and they have their own sanctity and obligations, but protecting the holy sites is our religious duty,” he said. Asif maintained that Muslims around the world did not need an agreement to act if the holy sites in Makkah or Madina came under attack. “There is no need to activate any agreement,” he said. The defence minister maintained that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. “There is absolutely no ambiguity,” he asserted. Asked about any military or political engagement with the Houthis, Asif said he could not disclose details, adding that strategies at this level were not meant to be made public. However, he reiterated that Pakistan was bound by the agreement. “Under the trilateral agreement, if the territorial integrity of a country comes under threat, the agreement will be activated and the other two countries will proceed to protect it in fulfilment of their obligations,” he said. “The situation has arrived.” On the US-Israeli war on Iran, Asif said it had become clear, a month into the conflict, that Israel’s calculations had not produced the expected results. “Israel sucked America into this war as a combatant party, but under the present circumstances, the world and the region need to realise that Israel is the real culprit,” he said. “Until Israel is confronted by a joint alliance, it will remain a threat to the region. The Zionist lobby also forces the US to join Israel’s wars.” Sharing his personal view on possible Iranian support for the Houthis, he said Iran, as a state, might not be backing the group as it was already embroiled in another conflict in the Middle East. “This would be a diplomatic error if Iran were to take the side of the Houthis, but the chances are minimal. Escalating the conflict into another theatre is not a wise decision and could turn it into a wider conflict,” Asif said. Fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Last week’s lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route. Pakistan’s stance Earlier today, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said that the defence alliance has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence. The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson. “It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said. Watson asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture. He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability. “It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. “This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence. “But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated. The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo. From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point. The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained.

story_clusters.representative_headline: India to take 'all necessary measures' to protect economic interests after US passes Russia sanctions bill

articles.headline: India to take 'all necessary measures' to protect economic interests after US passes Russia sanctions bill
articles.summary: India said on Thursday it would continue buying oil from “diversified” suppliers, after US lawmakers approved sanctions designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine. The US legislation targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. It also gives US President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas — including potentially China and India — in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war. But India’s foreign ministry said it “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people”. “It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.” Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners and military suppliers. “The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry added. India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran conflict in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in New Delhi last week ahead of a Brics summit. “This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors,” the ministry added. “Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.” Indian refiners nearly doubled crude imports from Russia to 2.25 million barrels a day in March — the weeks after the Middle East war erupted — helped by temporary US waivers. Shipments hit a record 2.81m in July, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler, but have since dropped back to 2.07m last month.

story_clusters.representative_headline: US Fed delivers first rate hike since 2023

articles.headline: US Fed delivers first rate hike since 2023
articles.summary: WASHINGTON: The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised interest rates in the world’s largest economy by 25 basis points to tackle stubbornly high inflation, a move sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has demanded lower rates. The Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent, citing “elevated” inflation and adding that the rate hike would support a “timelier return” to its 2pc target for the metric. Addressing a press conference after the rate decision, US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh stre­ssed that the central bank’s decision to raise interest rates, the first since 2023, was not influenced by financial markets. “We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation,” Warsh told the press conference. “I’ll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision.” He said that the central bank’s independence comes from staying focused on its objectives, in comments that come amid political pressure for lower interest rates. “Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane,” Warsh said. “We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them. “Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” he told a press conference. A majority of Fed policymakers expect at least one more rate hike to be necessary before the end of the year, according to the central bank’s Summary of Economic Projections, also published Wednesday. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

story_clusters.representative_headline: Capital Development Authority cancels 2,999-kanal Bahria Town layout plan

articles.headline: Capital Development Authority cancels 2,999-kanal Bahria Town layout plan
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD: The Capital Development Authority (CDA) has cancelled the layout plan of Bahria Town phases III-E and IV over alleged violations of the agreed plan, besides suspending processing and approval of other cases of the company “for being a defaulter”. According to a letter issued by the CDA’s Housing Directorate to the Bahria Town management, the layout plan of the two phases, spreading over 2,999-kanal, has been cancelled. The plan had been approved by the CDA in 2010 “subject to fulfillment of terms and conditions.” The letter alleged that Bahria Town had failed to fulfill terms and conditions and pre-requisite for obtaining NOC (no objection certificate) for the schemes, despite the lapse of about 15 years. It added that Bahria Town had been directed in 2025 to get all plots designated for public amenities, including parks, playgrounds, open spaces and public buildings, vacated and restore them in accordance with the approved layout plan. According to the CDA, the management of the scheme submitted a reply to the notice, but the authority did not accept it, terming it not based on facts. The CDA then issued a final show cause notice to the management in September last year. “Furthermore, DG of Federal Audit has framed Audit Para in 2023-24, titled, illegal construction of commercial building along Corniche Road, Bahria Town Phase III-E and IV, in Zone 5, without approval from CDA. The Departmental Account Committee headed by the secretary Ministry of Interior has discussed the para and ordered to remove such illegal commercial buildings, constructed in riverbed, graveyard and park/open space,” reads the notice. “Therefore, the layout plan approved dated 18-12-2010 is herby cancelled/withdrawn with immediate effect.” Besides this, the CDA has also decided to suspend “approval of other cases of Bahria Town (Pvt) Ltd, being defaulter of CDA”. Meanwhile, the CDA’s Housing Directorate has asked the enforcement wing of the authority “to take action for demolition/removed of works/buildings/structures constructed in this scheme”. An official of Bahria Town, when contacted, criticised the CDA’s decision, terming it ‘illegal’. “We submitted a revised layout plan for approval, but instead of granting approval, the CDA unilaterally canceled our previous layout plan … We will challenge this action before available forums including courts,” he said. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

story_clusters.representative_headline: IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nuclear power plant secured

articles.headline: IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nuclear power plant secured
articles.summary: • 1,200MW reactor’s dome placed early; commissioning set for 2028• Talks held with China on N-cooperation ISLAMABAD: The Inte­rnational Atomic Energy Agency and Pakistan on Wednesday signed a safeguards agreement for the 1,200-megawatt Chashma-5 nuclear power plant to bolster the country’s energy security while ensuring international non-proliferation standards. IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi and Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Raja Ali Raza Anwar signed the pact at the agency’s headquarters in Vienna. The signing took place on the sidelines of the 70th IAEA General Conference. Shan Zhongde, chairman of the China Atomic Energy Authority, witnessed the ceremony. The agreement, which governs the application of safeguards at Unit-5 of the Chashma plant, was unanimously approved by the IAEA Board of Governors in March. According to a statement on the signing, the agreement marks a critical step toward implementing safeguards for the new facility. Officials noted that it reflects the international community’s continued confidence in Pakistan’s commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy and its adherence to global non-proliferation obligations. Construction of the Chashma-5 (C-5) facility is progressing rapidly, with early completion of the reactor’s dome placement among its recent milestones. Scheduled for commissioning in 2028, the unit is expected to add a substantial source of low-carbon, low-cost electricity to Pakistan’s national grid to support climate objectives and sustainable economic growth. Pakistan currently operates six nuclear power plants with a combined installed capacity of 3,530 megawatts. According to the Atomic Energy Commission, these plants have maintained an average capacity factor exceeding 90pc. Officials highlighted that the country possesses more than 100 reactor-years of operational experience, maintaining a strong record of safe, secure and safeguarded operations under international standards. Prior to the signing ceremony, Pakistani and Chinese delegations met to discuss ongoing and future cooperation in the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. Anwar led the Pakistani delegation, while Zhongde headed the Chinese group. Mohammad Kamran Akhtar Malik, Pakistan’s ambassador to Austria and permanent representative to the IAEA, also participated in the bilateral discussions. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

story_clusters.representative_headline: African elephant Madhubala on ‘antibiotics’ after collapsing at Karachi’s Safari Park

articles.headline: African elephant Madhubala on ‘antibiotics’ after collapsing at Karachi’s Safari Park
articles.summary: KARACHI: Despite carrying out several tests, including an X-ray, over the past two days, the authorities in Safari Park remain clueless about what caused the sudden collapse of African elephant Madhubala in her enclosure, it emerged on Wednesday. Responding to queries, a spokesperson for the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) said that Madhubala suffered from “acute weakness and low immunity levels” following prolonged treatment for tuberculosis and that’s what caused her sudden fall. “While all her laboratory tests are just fine, she is being given antibiotics as a precautionary measure on the advice of a senior local vet. No fracture has been detected in the X-ray,” KMC spokesperson Daniyal Alishan Siyal told Dawn, adding that all medical reports were emailed to Sri Lankan wildlife health specialist Dr Buddhika for final assessment. When asked why she is being given antibiotics when no bacterial infection has been detected, he said, “I am told that she has elevated infection markers, though no specific cause has been detected.” The African elephant is suffering from ‘acute weakness and low immunity levels’ Madhubala, he pointed out, could now stand on her feet and the supporting crate belt had been removed. On the swelling on her right hind thigh, he claimed that, “It was caused by her fall.” He rejected the information that Madhubala was acutely dehydrated on the day of her fall because there wasn’t sufficient water to keep her cool on hot days. “There were no power breakdowns that could lead to water issues,” Mr Siyal said. Foot abscess recovery? Safari Park Director Amjad Zaidi two days ago stated that it’s apparently the swelling on her right thigh, which was preventing her from using her leg. He had also stated that Madhubala had “recovered” from a foot infection. Sources stated Madhubala’s swelling on her right hind thigh might be indicating spread of abscess from the foot (on the same affected leg) that she had been fighting for some period. “Elevated infection markers mean her body’s immune system is reacting to a problem, though her test results cannot tell the exact cause,” a senior vet shared. Steady signs of improvement: KMC The KMC released a press statement on Madhubala’s condition, stating that the elephant is showing steady signs of improvement and continues to receive round-the-clock veterinary care and close medical monitoring. “The latest health assessments have revealed several encouraging signs of improvement. Madhubala is now able to stand independently without harness support, marking a positive development in her recovery. Her vital parameters remain stable, while she continues to maintain a good appetite and remains alert and responsive,” it says. It further adds that Madhubala is undergoing daily health assessments and blood tests, while X-rays of her hind quarters are also being conducted regularly. “These diagnostic procedures are being carried out with the support of the Sindh Institute of Animal Health, enabling veterinary experts to closely monitor her physical condition and evaluate her progress. “Madhubala’s dedicated keeper team remains with her around the clock. The keepers, who have been closely involved in her daily care, are working in close coordination with the veterinary team to ensure that she receives appropriate nutrition, care, supervision and support throughout her recovery,” it adds. Madhubala had been in solitary confinement at Karachi Zoo following the tragic death of her companion Noor Jehan who died in 2023 after a tragic fall in her enclosure. Noor Jehan’s autopsy report released by the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) showed that she died from a severe blood parasitic infection and internal trauma combined with a lack of proper medical care. Left alone at the zoo, Madhubala was successfully relocated to Safari Park where she was reunited with her sisters, Sonia and Malika, in November 2024, under the supervision of Four Paws — an international animal welfare organisation that worked extensively with the KMC for elephant care. The success story of her reunion faded soon as Sonia died a month later after collapsing in her Safari enclosure. Lab reports later showed that she suffered from multiple chronic illnesses, affecting almost all vital organs, indicating prolonged neglect in her care and failure in timely diagnosis. Successive deaths of captive elephants raised public outcry, forcing the KMC to set up an 18-member body to look after Madhubala and Malika, both of whom were diagnosed with tuberculosis. The four female elephants were brought to Karachi from Tanzania in 2010 at a very young age under a controversial arrangement. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

story_clusters.representative_headline: ‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests Indian Navy vessel’s 'provocative' manoeuvre near PN vessel

articles.headline: ‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests Indian Navy vessel’s 'provocative' manoeuvre near PN vessel
articles.summary: Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the Charge d’Affaires of the Indian High Commission and lodged a “strong protest” over a “highly provocative and unacceptable” action by an Indian Navy vessel in Pakistan’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on Sept 15, the Foreign Office (FO) said. According to the FO, the incident occurred while the Pakistan Navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26. The FO said that the Indian vessel carried out “aggressive manoeuvres” in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels. The ministry termed the incident a “serious violation of international law” as well as the 1991 bilateral agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troop Movements. It said the incident also risked escalating tensions in the region. The Indian diplomat was asked to convey to New Delhi that Pakistan “strongly rejects” the “belligerent Indian action” and urged India to strictly adhere to international law and bilateral agreements, particularly those intended to prevent incidents at sea. The FO added that Pakistan’s Charge d’Affaires in New Delhi would lodge a similar demarche with India’s Ministry of External Affairs. Pakistan also called on the international community to urge India to refrain from what it described as “irresponsible actions” that could further destabilise South Asia. “The region can ill-afford to remain perpetually hostage to India’s reckless pursuit of conflict and instability,” the ministry said. India’s Ministry of External Affairs also summoned Pakistan’s envoy in New Delhi earlier today and issued a demarche over the incident. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan. Islamabad strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation. After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed six Indian planes in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight. After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire. In April, on the first anniversary of the Pahalgam attack, Pakistan had rejected a renewed Indian propaganda campaign linking it to the attack, deploring that the neighbouring country was focusing on “weaponising its false narrative” in the midst of a regional crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Yemeni forces clash with Houthis near Saudi border

articles.headline: Yemeni forces clash with Houthis near Saudi border
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters near the Saudi border, with AFP footage showing soldiers in armoured vehicles and trucks pushing across desert terrain under the crackle of machine-gun fire. The Houthis also released footage on Wednesday of the fighting in the Al-Jawf area, as well as a video purporting to show the downing of a fighter jet belonging to Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s main backer. “The First Division Emergency Forces are advancing on the Al-Labanat front and, God willing, will reach Houthi positions,” Waleed Al-Mahajeri, operations commander of the government’s Fifth Brigade, told an embedded AFP journalist on Tuesday. He went on to claim that the “Houthi militias are retreating and fleeing across all fronts”. AFP footage showed the soldiers firing heavy machine guns, artillery and RPGs at distant targets, as well as the bodies of Houthi fighters and entrenchments the government forces said the group had abandoned as they fell back. “Al-Masariya Hill has been liberated, as has Al-Labanat camp, and the advance is continuing towards Al-Tebab al-Soud,” said soldier Abu Mithaq. This handout picture released on September 16, 2026 by Ansarullah Media Centre shows what the Houthi authorities said is the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet that was shot down in the central province of Marib. — AFP Yemen’s civil war roared back to life in July after lying mostly dormant since 2022, with the Houthis making rapid advances that saw them seize the entirety of the country’s Red Sea coast and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the sea’s southern tip. The group has long held large parts of the country’s north, including the capital Sanaa. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have scrambled to respond to the new offensive, and Saudi airstrikes have failed to roll back the Houthis’ gains. In their own video, Houthi fighters can be seen racing across the desert in pick-up trucks, at one point firing on an advancing vehicle. “We are conducting now, God willing, an operation to… cut off the enemy,” one of the fighters can be heard saying. A separate video issued by the group includes night-vision footage appearing to show a projectile striking a fighter jet. Other scenes show the wreckage of a downed plane, with a charred tailfin bearing the Saudi flag. The Houthis said on Wednesday that they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet using a locally made missile. Earlier today, the Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthi rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. The Houthis swiftly rejected as a “lie” Riyadh’s report that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah, which attracts millions of pilgrims each year. “The claims about targeting Makkah are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone,” Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis’ politburo wrote on X.
