articles.headline: Asia News Network launches new e-book celebrating continent's cultural heritage
articles.summary: The Asia News Network (ANN), an alliance of 20 leading news titles across the continent, has released a new e-book dedicated to celebrating the cultural heritage, modern innovation, and enduring spirit of Asia. The e-book, titled Inside Asia’s Hidden Heritage Treasures, aims to offer global and regional readers an authentic glimpse into the continent’s shared identity, according to a press release. The publication explores Unesco heritage sites, tourism attractions both ancient and modern, Asia’s best-kept secrets and unique cultural treasures. Current ANN Chairperson and Malaysia’s Star Media Group Chief Content Officer Datin Paduka Esther Ng said the e-book celebrated Asia’s unique ability to rapidly modernise, while deeply honouring its roots. “Asia is living proof of heritage and legacy living on and evolving,” Ng said, adding that the region seamlessly blends ancient legacies with ultra-modern facets and the fastest technology adoption in the world. “Ng highlighted that the e-book’s focus on Asia’s winning factors that foster global togetherness, and adds that the region has inherited a priceless form of heritage defined by endurance and survival — two traits that she views as the most accurate descriptions of the Asian experience,” the press release said. The e-book also addresses the long-standing challenge of relying on Western perspectives to tell Asian stories. Former ANN chairman Mahfuz Anam, editor-in-chief and publisher of Bangladesh’s The Daily Star, was quoted as saying that the network was founded 27 years ago to correct this imbalance, calling the new e-book an integral part of a “journey of rediscovery”.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Govt working to introduce virtual grid system, says power minister

articles.headline: Govt working to introduce virtual grid system, says power minister
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD: Power Minister Awais Leghari on Wednesday said the government was working to introduce a virtual grid system in the country, under which consumers would be able to generate and store electricity. Talking to the media after a National Assembly panel meeting, the minister said work on regulations for virtual grids had already started and that the regulations would be finalised by the last quarter of the current fiscal year. The minister said power distribution companies (Discos) had also been directed to install batteries on their grids as part of efforts to improve the power system and promote energy storage. “A battery revolution is coming to Pakistan as the government seeks to promote battery use and introduce a virtual grid system,” he said. “The government’s objective is to increase the use of batteries in the country’s power sector.” Earlier, the minister faced a tough time at the NA Standing Committee on Power meeting as committee chairman Muhammad Idrees questioned him about prolonged electricity load-shedding in the country. During the meeting, Leghari acknowledged that load-shedding was being carried out on around 3,500 of the country’s 14,500 feeders due to electricity theft and line losses. “Within a year, the government will shift load-shedding from feeders to transformers so that an entire feeder will not have to be shut down,” he said, adding that the government was also introducing an on-off control system for around 190,000 transformers. With the new system, he said, it would not be necessary to shut down an entire feeder, while consumers who regularly paid their electricity bills would not be affected. He said there was currently no additional load-shedding in the country. “The outages are mainly occurring due to faults caused by overloading of the power system.” Leghari said heavy investment was required to upgrade the power system and that approval from the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) would be sought for the upgrades. Regarding the energy situation, the minister said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had affected the Petroleum Division’s ability to receive LNG cargoes. He said the government was using locally produced gas for power generation. Explaining the decision to carry out load-shedding at night, Leghari asked, “Who will bear an additional electricity bill of Rs6 to Rs6.50 per unit?” He said a gas cargo that previously cost around $30 million was now costing more than $95 million, making it necessary to take measures to reduce fuel costs. “We carried out load-shedding during peak hours to save fuel costs,” the minister said. He clarified that the government had not signed any new agreement with any independent power producer (IPP), adding that incorrect reports had appeared in the media on the matter. During the meeting, PML-N MNA Rana Muhammad Hayat said there was a lot of discussion but electricity prices had not come down. “There is so much load-shedding that it has become difficult for us to go among the people,” he said. Hayat also criticised the performance of the Discos, but ended up blaming the policymakers and the ministry for the state of affairs in the power sector. “What can the Discos do, minister sahab? You switch off the electricity,” he said. The PML-N lawmaker said the government’s policies gave the impression that it was working primarily to meet the requirements of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), rather than addressing people’s problems. “Yes, I feel like we are working not for the country but only for the IMF,” he said. The minister, however, responded that Hayat was making an irresponsible statement at a responsible forum.

story_clusters.representative_headline: PHF requests AHF to shift Asian Champions Trophy out of India or relocate Pakistan matches

articles.headline: PHF requests AHF to shift Asian Champions Trophy out of India or relocate Pakistan matches
articles.summary: The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) has formally asked the Asian Hockey Federation (AHF) to move next month’s men’s Asian Champions Trophy out of India or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue, citing the “sensitive bilateral situation” between the two countries. The request effectively rules out Pakistan playing their matches at the tournament’s scheduled venues in Jalandhar and Mohali unless the AHF agrees to the proposed change. PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani, who is also federal secretary of the Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination, confirmed to Dawn on Wednesday that the federation had formally approached the AHF. The development came two days after Wani had told Dawn that Pakistan’s proposed tour to India was subject to government clearance and that the PHF would abide by whatever decision the government took. Sources in the PHF said the latest decision to seek a neutral venue had been taken on the direction of the federal government. In an official statement issued on Wednesday, Wani said the request had been made to ensure a “safe, dignified and conducive environment” for Pakistan’s players and officials. “The Pakistan Hockey Federation has formally requested the Asian Hockey Federation to relocate the Men’s Asian Champions Trophy 2026 tournament or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue,” Wani said in the statement. The PHF chief, however, made it clear that Pakistan remained committed to the tournament and was willing to face India. “Pakistan remains fully committed to participating in the Asian Champions Trophy and international hockey and is ready to play against all FIH member nations, including India,” he said. The PHF president also said the federation hoped the AHF would consider the proposal positively to ensure Pakistan’s full participation in the tournament. The request comes two days after Indian Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said Pakistan would participate in the tournament, prompting the PHF to clarify that no decision had been taken on the team’s visit to India. Mann, according to a Press Trust of India (PTI) report, had said Pakistan would be among the six teams competing in the Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held from Oct 27 to Nov 5. “There is no problem in multi-national tournaments. Maybe individual series [between India and Pakistan] cannot take place,” Mann said at an event in Mohali when asked about Pakistan’s participation and whether the requisite clearances had been obtained. The tournament is scheduled to feature hosts India, Pakistan, China, Japan, Malaysia and South Korea. Jalandhar is to host the opening ceremony and all league-stage matches from Oct 27 to Nov 2, while the semi-finals and final are scheduled to be played in Mohali on Nov 4 and 5. Pakistan’s proposed match against India is scheduled for Nov 1 in Jalandhar. The PHF’s latest move means that, while Pakistan is seeking to avoid playing its fixtures in India, it is not seeking to withdraw from the competition. The federation has specifically stated that it is prepared to play India and other FIH member nations at a neutral venue. Pakistan had also withdrawn from last year’s Junior World Cup in Tamil Nadu amid heightened tensions between the two countries.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Indian delegates attempt to interrupt Ayaz Sadiq’s address at Commonwealth conference

articles.headline: Indian delegates attempt to interrupt Ayaz Sadiq’s address at Commonwealth conference
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD: Indian delegates reportedly attempted to interrupt National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq’s address at the 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Cape Town, South Africa, as he spoke about climate adaptation and climate justice. According to information available, the Indian delegates repeatedly sought to intervene during Sadiq’s speech, with footage showing attempts to get hold of the microphone and disrupt the proceedings. Sadiq had raised the issue of “water terrorism” during his address without naming any country, in the context of broader concerns over climate change, water resources and climate justice. The Indian delegates’ attempts to seize the microphone affected the atmosphere of the session, prompting direct intervention by the host and the Jamaican speaker, who asked them either to remain silent or leave the hall. Meanwhile, other participants advised the Indian delegates to listen patiently to Speaker Sadiq’s address. Despite the disruption, the discussion on climate adaptation and climate justice continued. In his address, Speaker Sadiq, without naming any country or delegation, presented a principled position on tackling climate change and stressed the responsibilities of the international community. He raised issues, including the sudden surge of water in rivers and the withholding of water, without naming any country. Speaker Sadiq said climate adaptation policies should be formulated with effective public participation, adding that oversight by democratic institutions was indispensable to policies aimed at addressing climate change. He added that climate change was affecting various spheres of life, including food, water and health, noting that Pakistan was among the countries most affected by climate change. “Tackling climate change requires climate justice and the inclusion of democratic institutions,” he said, adding that parliamentary dialogue on global challenges such as climate change should be serious, purposeful and constructive. He said the role of parliaments was important in the practical implementation of climate policies and that international climate finance should come under parliamentary oversight. “The Parliament of Pakistan is playing an important role in climate adaptation through legislation, budgetary oversight and committees,” he said, adding that the inclusion of women, youth and other segments of society was indispensable to addressing climate change. “To deal with climate risks, parliaments should benefit from mutual experiences,” he said, adding that to meet the challenges of climate change, parliaments should promote cooperation and meaningful dialogue rather than differences. “Strong democratic institutions are indispensable for strong and vibrant societies,” Speaker Sadiq said, adding that climate adaptation could be effective only with fair financial assistance and democratic accountability. The Indus Water Treaty (IWT) remains a contentious issue between Pakistan and India, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year — a move that was followed by a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025. Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. In August, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in the Hague also ordered India to uphold the IWT with Pakistan and suspend work on a hydro project in occupied Kashmir.

story_clusters.representative_headline: South Africa pushes back on US visa curbs

articles.headline: South Africa pushes back on US visa curbs
articles.summary: South Africa on Wednesday hit back at new US visa restrictions over its racial equity policies, accusing the Trump administration of distorting its laws and further straining ties between Washington and one of Africa’s most influential powers. The dispute is the latest front in a broader clash over race, trade and diplomacy that has seen Washington cut aid, impose tariffs, expel South Africa’s ambassador and boycott a G20 summit in Johannesburg, all against the unresolved legacy of white minority rule. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the new visa restrictions would target those who promote “race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said Pretoria viewed the move “with concern” and that Washington was echoing narratives promoted by fringe groups opposed to South Africa’s post-apartheid reforms. “We reiterate that healing the divisions of the past and establishing a society based on democratic values, social justice and fundamental human rights is a constitutional imperative,” Lamola said in a statement. The US did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions but warned of further “severe” action. “This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter,” US ambassador to South Africa, Brent Bozell, said. ‘Hypocrisy’ President Donald Trump has criticised South Africa’s land reform and employment equity laws, which were introduced after the end of apartheid to address racial disparities that remain among the world’s widest. Trump has portrayed the measures as discriminatory against Afrikaners, the white minority descended largely from Dutch settlers, a claim Pretoria rejects. In 2025, he berated President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a “white genocide” in South Africa. While the US president has broadly cracked down on immigration, his administration has offered refugee status to thousands of white South Africans it says face persecution. Lamola rejected suggestions that the government was targeting any racial group, saying crime remained a national challenge affecting all South Africans. The opposition uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party, led by former president Jacob Zuma, also condemned the visa restrictions, calling them an affront to South Africa’s sovereignty. “The hypocrisy of Washington’s position is breathtaking. It lectures South Africa, while arming Israel amid the reported killing of more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza,” it said in a statement. Despite the tensions, Pretoria and Washington have remained engaged in efforts to thaw relations. “The discussions have highlighted the need for any resolution to consider South Africa’s unique circumstances and to respect its democracy, constitution, sovereignty, and the will of its people,” Lamola said. South Africa is the largest trading partner of the US on the African continent, with more than 500 US businesses and 30,000 US citizens based in the country. South Africa said last month it would offer a “generous” new trade deal to the United States as it seeks to avoid hefty tariffs that threaten job losses on top of a dire unemployment crisis.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Some critical questions

articles.headline: Some critical questions
articles.summary: TRUE to tradition, a ‘plan’ to ‘reset’ the country’s entire structure has come down like an epiphany from apparently ‘non-political’ quarters. The plan envisages creating multiple provinces and changing the country’s very tapestry — its geography, topography, demography, ethnic relations, resource distribution, power sharing, and broader political calculus. The situation raises critical questions. Why new provinces? The interior minister, who announced the plan, hasn’t held forth on the reasoning or offered an acceptable justification for adopting such an extreme and hazardous course. However, he has mentioned bad governance, population implosion, and systemic failures as some of the causes. Nor are there any official authoritative studies proposing a close nexus between good governance and smaller administrative structures. In fact, the global landscape reveals a mixed pattern. Some countries have fewer or territorially larger constituent units, and yet they are stable, functional, even enviable. Others have multiple small units/ provinces, but are perennially afflicted with broken, inept and even failed political systems. The factors that generally determine the performance and vitality of a state are the legitimacy and efficacy of its political system, the character and ability of its leadership, and the maturity and capacity of its institutions — not only to deliver better governance, but also to meet the continuing challenges thrown up by ever-changing societal and state imperatives. In revitalising the ‘failed’ political systems, we don’t know if the so-called plan contemplates these factors. Who is demanding them? Interestingly, most of these ideas have originated outside regular political processes, whether as One Unit, Basic Democracy, ‘Islamisation’, enlightened moderation, or hybrid governance. People have always been on the receiving end of new-fangled ideas and their pernicious consequences. The call for a structural ‘reset’, too, appears to have similar origins. So far, none of the governments — federal, provincial or even local — or the mainstream political leaderships have called for restructuring the provinces. However, there is near-consensus across the political spectrum on creating provinces in south Punjab, and KP’s Hazara belt. In fact, the Punjab and KP assemblies passed resolutions for these provinces, but they went nowhere. Instead of new units, the country needs softer options to heal societal wounds. Reorganising the state structures would be an extremely risky exercise. India’s Congress party had included the ‘linguistic’ provinces in its manifesto as early as 1917. Yet, after Partition, both prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru and home minister Vallabhbhai Patel were reluctant to reorganise the states, fearing balkanisation of the fledgling country. It was many months of intense political agitations across the country, expert studies, judicial commissions, and a much-mourned fast unto death by Telugu nationalist Potti Sriramulu that finally brought the government around. Still, the Reorganisation Act of 1955 was not passed to improve governance but to group various linguistic communities in their own separate states. In other words, distinctive ethno-cultural identities were recognised and restored, rather than brutally denied and suppressed as would have been the case if the states had been broken up in a manner that dispersed the historically located ethno-cultural communities — something that is being contemplated here. Is referendum feasible? Perhaps encouraged by the smooth passage of the controversial 26th and 27th constitutional amendments, and not expecting a large section of the political establishment to oppose the proposed move, some elements here had appeared confident of securing the required numbers to ensure restructuring. However, the JUI-F, ANP, PTI, and even the ruling party’s major coalition partner have dug in their heels. In fact, even the prime minister and his party seem reluctant to support the restructuring, though some government ministers are backing it, albeit without the cabinet’s approval. Likewise, the Sindh Assembly has also rejected the break-up of the province. As a result, other means are being sought — preferably, a referendum to execute the plan. But a referendum would not validate the wholesale reorganisation of the state. It lacks legitimacy and credibility. It cannot be used to circumvent or be a substitute for the mandatory constitutional amendment. People will not accept it because every military dictator has used it to legitimise their rule. Instead, a referendum will be seen as farcical and incite public anger, triggering a maelstrom of pushback. Will the ‘plan’ succeed? Any idea, policy, or law that is imposed on the people has miserably failed to achieve its objectives; in fact, it has often led to disasters. Steamrolling the restructuring of provinces — against the will of the people — will further aggravate identity-driven politics across a fragile multiethnic landscape. It may even ignite the tinderbox the country has become, particularly for poor and disgruntled youth who have endured the harrowing realities of failed systems. The numbers are dreadful. Half the population lives in poverty, around 28 million children are out of school, four out of 10 children suffer from stunted growth, three-fourths of the populace is consuming contaminated water, and the increasingly murky security environment scares away local and foreign investors. In these dire circumstances, the country desperately needs softer options to heal societal wounds — options that recompense the people through justice, equity, peace, opportunity, and development, which are democracy’s tested tools. The yawning fault lines — ethnic, social, political, inter-provincial and centre-province — must be mended, and federal democracy, which remains buried under the hybrid regime, restored. The system does need a ‘reset’. But the reset should mean building efficient and accountable institutions, strengthening rules-based governance, and allowing legitimate and representative leadership to run political and public offices. That requires a continuous process of fair, free elections held on time, so that dead wood can be replaced with a fresher, cleaner leadership at the federal, provincial, and local levels. Finally, a ‘reset’ would be fatal if it ignored the emotional, even spiritual, bonding of the various ethno-cultural communities with their respective provinces. This bonding goes beyond ideology or politics. It is the product of the centuries-long interplay between these communities and their distinctive land, history, culture, language, literature and art. This bonding leads many in Sindh to conceive their province as an indivisible historical entity — a firmer federalised version of Scotland or Quebec. The writer is a lawyer. shahabusto@hotmail.com Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

articles.headline: ‘New pathway for the future’: Quantum Valley Pakistan launched in Islamabad
articles.summary: Quantum Valley Pakistan, a project likened to America’s Silicon Valley, was launched in Islamabad on Wednesday, with Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal as the chief guest. The Planning Ministry described Quantum Valley Pakistan as a project aimed at connecting academia, entrepreneurs, government and investors to turn “knowledge into solutions, startups into scalable ventures and innovation into national impact”. The project aims to create new pathways for Pakistani talent in AI, quantum computing, fintech, agritech, biotechnology, medtech, digital solutions and autonomous technologies, the ministry said. California’s venture capital firm Plug and Play and the Cambridge Innovation Centre collaborated with the government for the project. Addressing the launch ceremony, Iqbal said, “We are actually setting a new pathway for Pakistan’s future”. “Pakistan is ready for innovation takeoff,” he said. He stressed that this was not an ordinary collaboration, adding that the two companies would bring to Pakistan the “best of innovation in the world and the United States”. Describing the collaboration as a “unique opportunity” for Pakistan, Iqbal expressed hope for the growth of the country’s technology sector. He said that the paradigm of national progress had shifted in the 21st century, with “brain power” now being a key requirement for development. The planning minister added that the foundations for growth being established through Quantum Valley would allow Pakistan’s youth to compete with the youth of the world in terms of tech growth and startups. “Today, we stand at an inflection point,” Iqbal said, adding that in the past two years, Pakistan had seen many successes, namely Marka-i-Haq and recent diplomacy efforts in the US-Iran war. “In my lifetime, I had never seen that for an entire week, media from the US to Australia was only mentioning Islamabad,” he said, referring to the Islamabad talks in April. Successes achieved in defence and diplomacy, if not supplemented by a strong economy, can blur over time, Iqbal said. Alluding to Marka-i-Haq, Iqbal said the nation had to rise to the occasion of “Marka-i-Taraqi” and aim to build a $1 trillion economy by 2035 under the Uraan Pakistan programme. He further said the economy should grow to $3 trillion by 2047, when the country marks its centenary. Uraan Pakistan is an initiative of the Planning Ministry designed to advance key projects and reforms set out in the 5Es National Economic Transformation Plan. “These goals are ambitious but not impossible,” Iqbal said. Iqbal urged the nation to move away from the status quo and instead opt for a “transformational path”. The ceremony also included the inauguration of the Global Venture Acceleration Programme for local startups, under which they would receive mentorship over 15 weeks, along with a two-week global immersion in Silicon Valley or Boston.
